# Challenge: Industrial Metaverse (Valmet)

Summary of the official brief, which is the docx in `Valmet_SinceAI2026 _1_/` (not in git).
Questions go to the Since AI Discord challenge channel.

## What to build
Focus on backend and spatial processing. No mobile app, and keep the UI lightweight.

1. **Extract assets:** detect and put 3D boxes around as many objects as possible in
   `Industrial Boiler Room.ply`.
2. **Map metadata:** link extracted assets to the Excel pack. Random or procedural mapping is
   allowed, with a pre-determined faulty target device.
3. **Navigate:** a worker or robot follows an automatic, collision-free route on the floor to the
   faulty device.
4. **Show nearby assets:** highlight 3D boxes and metadata for assets near the avatar as it moves.
5. **Diagnose:** on arrival, an AI assistant explains the fault and recommends next steps, grounded
   in the Excel pack.

## Scoring
| Weight | Criterion |
|---|---|
| 30% | Number and quality of extracted, 3D-framed assets mapped to metadata |
| 25% | Realistic obstacle-free navigation and proximity display |
| 20% | AI diagnostics, grounding and explainability |
| 15% | Backend architecture: structured, automated, modular |
| 10% | Demo clarity and innovation |

## Submission
- Working demo, runnable locally or clearly recorded
- Repo with a concise README and setup instructions
- 5-8 slides: extraction pipeline, pathfinding, metadata mapping, AI approach
- Demo video, 5 minutes maximum
- Brief technical note on models, libraries, and software

## Data
| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `Industrial Boiler Room (1).ply` | Gaussian splat, spherical harmonics degree 3 (45 `f_rest`) |
| `Industrial Boiler Room (1).mp4` | 1080p walkthrough, 3,352 frames, 112 s, no camera poses supplied |
| `semantic extraction demo 1/2` | Reference videos of the desired output (different sites) |
| `Valmet_..._Builder_Pack (1)...xlsx` | 30 assets, states, alarms, work orders, service cases, docs |

Asset classes: 12 control valves, 6 pumps, 6 motors, 3 pressure transmitters, 3 vibration sensors.
The pack is synthetic. Its `Scene_Anchors` coordinates are placeholders, not real scene positions.

AI answers must follow the pack's rules: `DOC-RAG-GUIDE` (name the asset, cite evidence IDs, give
confidence, separate observation from hypothesis), `DOC-FIELD-SAFETY` (recommend verification, not
autonomous action), and `DOC-3D-MAPPING` (never silently guess identity, so store how each asset
was mapped and with what confidence).

## Known data problems (as of 2026-11-06)
- **The PLY looks damaged.** Records 0-502,481 are valid (unit quaternions, plausible values). The
  other 1,003,654 records, 67% of the file, look like random bytes, including NaN and values near
  1e36. The file size matches its header. Cause unknown. SHA-256 starts `117195366421b07a`.
- **Until replaced, load only the first 502,482 records.** Of those, 35,635 have opacity above 0.5.
  Their extent is about 8.7 x 2.7 x 4.4 scene units, with y the thin axis (probably vertical), so
  this may be only part of the room.
- **Files the pack mentions are missing:** `telemetry_full_14d_30min.csv` (the workbook has a 3-day
  sample) and the 38 RAG markdown files (the workbook has 8 core docs).

Written for you, except the Discord draft, which is for Valmet.

**Probably not as a replacement, at least without Valmet's OK.** I noted that the brief is built around their file, but I still pushed the reconstruction too hard, and it should have stayed a fallback.

## What the brief says
- **Their file is required:** you must submit a demonstrator "using `Industrial Boiler Room.ply`", and at minimum it must "process" that file.
- **The freedom is about tools:** "technical freedom" covers languages and visualizers, not the input scene.
- **The scoring names it too:** the top criterion is how well you process that file, and the demo video must show navigation in it.
- **The video isn't in the brief's starter list:** `Industrial Boiler Room.mp4` was in your package but isn't listed in the brief, which gives no guidance on using it.

So a swap risks being judged as not meeting the minimum, though their damaged file is a good reason to ask for an exception.

## What I'd do now
1. **Build on their PLY:** use the valid records for loading, cleaning, extraction and routing. That work counts whatever Valmet answers.
2. **Ask Valmet today:** send the draft below.
3. **Hold the reconstruction:** Pi³ and 3DGS wait for their answer. The frames are already on Roihu, so nothing is lost, and a fixed `.ply` would make them unnecessary.

If Valmet fixes the file, use it. If they can't but approve a reconstruction, say so openly in the demo and technical note. Using the video only to help label objects in their scene might be acceptable too, which is why the draft asks about it.

> 2. If it can't be fixed, may we reconstruct the scene from `Industrial Boiler Room.mp4`, or should we use only the valid part?
> 3. Even with a good `.ply`, may we use the video frames to help label objects in the scene?
> 4. The builder pack mentions `telemetry_full_14d_30min.csv` and 38 RAG markdown files that weren't in our package. Are those available?

# Challenge: Industrial Metaverse (Valmet)

Summary of the official brief, which is the docx in `Valmet_SinceAI2026 _1_/` (not in git).
Questions go to the Since AI Discord challenge channel.

## What to build
Focus on backend and spatial processing. No mobile app, and keep the UI lightweight.

1. **Extract assets:** detect and put 3D boxes around as many objects as possible in
   `Industrial Boiler Room.ply`.
2. **Map metadata:** link extracted assets to the Excel pack. Random or procedural mapping is
   allowed, with a pre-determined faulty target device.
3. **Navigate:** a worker or robot follows an automatic, collision-free route on the floor to the
   faulty device.
4. **Show nearby assets:** highlight 3D boxes and metadata for assets near the avatar as it moves.
5. **Diagnose:** on arrival, an AI assistant explains the fault and recommends next steps, grounded
   in the Excel pack.

## Scoring
| Weight | Criterion |
|---|---|
| 30% | Number and quality of extracted, 3D-framed assets mapped to metadata |
| 25% | Realistic obstacle-free navigation and proximity display |
| 20% | AI diagnostics, grounding and explainability |
| 15% | Backend architecture: structured, automated, modular |
| 10% | Demo clarity and innovation |

## Submission
- Working demo, runnable locally or clearly recorded
- Repo with a concise README and setup instructions
- 5-8 slides: extraction pipeline, pathfinding, metadata mapping, AI approach
- Demo video, 5 minutes maximum
- Brief technical note on models, libraries, and software

## Data
| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `Industrial Boiler Room (1).ply` | Gaussian splat, spherical harmonics degree 3 (45 `f_rest`) |
| `Industrial Boiler Room (1).mp4` | 1080p walkthrough, 3,352 frames, 112 s, no camera poses supplied |
| `semantic extraction demo 1/2` | Reference videos of the desired output (different sites) |
| `Valmet_..._Builder_Pack (1)...xlsx` | 30 assets, states, alarms, work orders, service cases, docs |

Asset classes: 12 control valves, 6 pumps, 6 motors, 3 pressure transmitters, 3 vibration sensors.
The pack is synthetic. Its `Scene_Anchors` coordinates are placeholders, not real scene positions.

AI answers must follow the pack's rules: `DOC-RAG-GUIDE` (name the asset, cite evidence IDs, give
confidence, separate observation from hypothesis), `DOC-FIELD-SAFETY` (recommend verification, not
autonomous action), and `DOC-3D-MAPPING` (never silently guess identity, so store how each asset
was mapped and with what confidence).

## Scene input rule
The brief requires a demonstrator "using" `Industrial Boiler Room.ply`, and the minimum demo must
"process" it. Its technical freedom covers languages and visualization tools, not the input scene.
Its starter package list doesn't mention `Industrial Boiler Room.mp4`, though the file was supplied.
Our own reconstruction from that video is not an approved replacement unless Valmet confirms it.

## Known data problems (as of 2026-11-06)
- **The PLY looks damaged.** Records 0-502,481 are valid (unit quaternions, plausible values). The
  other 1,003,654 records, 67% of the file, look like random bytes, including NaN and values near
  1e36. The file size matches its header. Cause unknown. SHA-256 starts `117195366421b07a`.
- **Until replaced, load only the first 502,482 records.** Of those, 35,635 have opacity above 0.5.
  Their extent is about 8.7 x 2.7 x 4.4 scene units, with y the thin axis (probably vertical), so
  this may be only part of the room.
- **Files the pack mentions are missing:** `telemetry_full_14d_30min.csv` (the workbook has a 3-day
  sample) and the 38 RAG markdown files (the workbook has 8 core docs).

"""Reconstruct cameras and points from frames with Pi3X, for comparison against Valmet's PLY.

    python scripts/reconstruct_pi3.py FRAMES_DIR OUT_DIR --weights WEIGHTS_DIR --frames 100

Needs a GPU and the `pi3` package. Writes points.ply, cameras.npz and summary.json.
"""

import argparse
import json
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch
from pi3.models.pi3x import Pi3X
from pi3.utils.basic import load_images_as_tensor


def write_ply(path: Path, xyz: np.ndarray, rgb: np.ndarray) -> None:
    vertex = np.empty(
        len(xyz),
        dtype=[("x", "<f4"), ("y", "<f4"), ("z", "<f4"), ("r", "u1"), ("g", "u1"), ("b", "u1")],
    )
    vertex["x"], vertex["y"], vertex["z"] = xyz.T
    vertex["r"], vertex["g"], vertex["b"] = rgb.T
    header = (
        "ply\nformat binary_little_endian 1.0\n"
        f"element vertex {len(xyz)}\n"
        "property float x\nproperty float y\nproperty float z\n"
        "property uchar red\nproperty uchar green\nproperty uchar blue\nend_header\n"
    )
    with path.open("wb") as file:
        file.write(header.encode())
        vertex.tofile(file)


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("frames_dir", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("out_dir", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("--weights", type=Path, required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--frames", type=int, default=100)
    parser.add_argument("--min-confidence", type=float, default=0.5)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    args.out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    available = len(list(args.frames_dir.glob("*.jpg")))
    interval = max(available // args.frames, 1)
    images = load_images_as_tensor(str(args.frames_dir), interval=interval)[: args.frames]

    start = time.perf_counter()
    model = Pi3X.from_pretrained(str(args.weights)).to("cuda").eval()
    load_seconds = time.perf_counter() - start

    start = time.perf_counter()
    with torch.no_grad(), torch.amp.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        output = model(images.cuda()[None])
    infer_seconds = time.perf_counter() - start

    points = output["points"][0].float().cpu().numpy()
    confidence = torch.sigmoid(output["conf"][0, ..., 0]).float().cpu().numpy()
    poses = output["camera_poses"][0].float().cpu().numpy()
    colors = (images.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).numpy() * 255).astype(np.uint8)

    keep = confidence > args.min_confidence
    write_ply(args.out_dir / "points.ply", points[keep], colors[keep])
    np.savez_compressed(args.out_dir / "cameras.npz", camera_to_world=poses)

    centers = poses[:, :3, 3]
    summary = {
        "frames": len(images),
        "frame_interval": interval,
        "image_size_hw": list(images.shape[-2:]),
        "gpu": torch.cuda.get_device_name(0),
        "load_seconds": round(load_seconds, 1),
        "infer_seconds": round(infer_seconds, 1),
        "peak_gpu_gb": round(torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9, 1),
        "points_kept": int(keep.sum()),
        "points_total": int(keep.size),
        "bounds_min": np.percentile(points[keep], 0.5, axis=0).round(2).tolist(),
        "bounds_max": np.percentile(points[keep], 99.5, axis=0).round(2).tolist(),
        "camera_path_length": round(float(np.linalg.norm(np.diff(centers, axis=0), axis=1).sum()), 2),
        "metric": float(output["metric"].float().cpu().numpy().reshape(-1)[0]),
    }
    (args.out_dir / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))
    print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Reconstruct cameras and points from frames with Pi3X, for comparison against Valmet's PLY.

    python scripts/reconstruct_pi3.py FRAMES_DIR OUT_DIR --weights WEIGHTS_DIR --frames 100

Needs a GPU and the `pi3` package. Writes points.ply, cameras.npz and summary.json.
"""

import argparse
import json
import time
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import torch
from pi3.models.pi3x import Pi3X
from pi3.utils.basic import load_images_as_tensor


def write_ply(path: Path, xyz: np.ndarray, rgb: np.ndarray) -> None:
    vertex = np.empty(
        len(xyz),
        dtype=[("x", "<f4"), ("y", "<f4"), ("z", "<f4"), ("r", "u1"), ("g", "u1"), ("b", "u1")],
    )
    vertex["x"], vertex["y"], vertex["z"] = xyz.T
    vertex["r"], vertex["g"], vertex["b"] = rgb.T
    header = (
        "ply\nformat binary_little_endian 1.0\n"
        f"element vertex {len(xyz)}\n"
        "property float x\nproperty float y\nproperty float z\n"
        "property uchar red\nproperty uchar green\nproperty uchar blue\nend_header\n"
    )
    with path.open("wb") as file:
        file.write(header.encode())
        vertex.tofile(file)


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("frames_dir", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("out_dir", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("--weights", type=Path, required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--frames", type=int, default=100)
    parser.add_argument("--min-confidence", type=float, default=0.5)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    args.out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    available = len(list(args.frames_dir.glob("*.jpg")))
    interval = max(available // args.frames, 1)
    images = load_images_as_tensor(str(args.frames_dir), interval=interval)[: args.frames]

    start = time.perf_counter()
    model = Pi3X.from_pretrained(str(args.weights)).to("cuda").eval()
    load_seconds = time.perf_counter() - start

    start = time.perf_counter()
    with torch.no_grad(), torch.amp.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        output = model(images.cuda()[None])
    infer_seconds = time.perf_counter() - start

    points = output["points"][0].float().cpu().numpy()
    confidence = torch.sigmoid(output["conf"][0, ..., 0]).float().cpu().numpy()
    poses = output["camera_poses"][0].float().cpu().numpy()
    colors = (images.permute(0, 2, 3, 1).numpy() * 255).astype(np.uint8)

    keep = confidence > args.min_confidence
    write_ply(args.out_dir / "points.ply", points[keep], colors[keep])
    np.savez_compressed(args.out_dir / "cameras.npz", camera_to_world=poses)

    centers = poses[:, :3, 3]
    summary = {
        "frames": len(images),
        "frame_interval": interval,
        "image_size_hw": list(images.shape[-2:]),
        "gpu": torch.cuda.get_device_name(0),
        "load_seconds": round(load_seconds, 1),
        "infer_seconds": round(infer_seconds, 1),
        "peak_gpu_gb": round(torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 1e9, 1),
        "points_kept": int(keep.sum()),
        "points_total": int(keep.size),
        "bounds_min": np.percentile(points[keep], 0.5, axis=0).round(2).tolist(),
        "bounds_max": np.percentile(points[keep], 99.5, axis=0).round(2).tolist(),
        "camera_path_length": round(float(np.linalg.norm(np.diff(centers, axis=0), axis=1).sum()), 2),
        "metric": float(output["metric"].float().cpu().numpy().reshape(-1)[0]),
    }
    (args.out_dir / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))
    print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.text:
**The Pi³X test ran successfully and the result is promising, but it's not good enough to use as a scene yet.** The job itself took about a minute on one L40.

| Measure | Result |
|---|---|
| **Frames** | 100, about 1 in 15 of your selection |
| **Image size** | 672 × 378 |
| **Inference time** | 15.6 s |
| **Peak GPU memory** | 29.2 GB of about 45 GB free |
| **Points above 0.5 confidence** | 1.73 million, about 7% of the total |

## How it looks
- **Good:**
    - The floor comes out large and flat, which routing needs. Your pipes, pallet jack, crates and blue tank are all recognisable.
    - The camera height stays steady across the walkthrough.
- **Bad:**
    - From above, the room looks like separate patches that may not line up, so the overall layout isn't proven.
    - There are stripe artifacts on surfaces seen at shallow angles, and the upper part of the room is largely missing, possibly because of the confidence cutoff.
- **Likely causes:** 100 frames is sparse, with camera jumps of up to about 3.3 units between frames. More frames might help, but that's untested.
- **Scale:** I don't yet know whether the point coordinates are in metres, so don't read real sizes from this.

To look for yourself, see `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-viktor-trilar-Projects-Newbies/6293938d-e68f-4310-92b7-6bf722e3d028/scratchpad/pi3_100/top.png` and `front.png` in the same folder. They're rough plots of the points, not rendered splats.

## What this means for the comparison
- **Memory limit:** at this resolution, roughly 150 frames should fit in one Pi³X run, based on simple scaling from this test. So all 1,500 can't go through at once, and would have to be split into chunks and aligned, which can introduce drift.
- **Better next test:** COLMAP can use all 1,500 frames at full resolution, and it should show whether the layout holds together. If it does, those cameras can feed 3DGS. If it fails, a Pi³X run on about 150 frames is the fallback.

I'd run this as a CPU job on Roihu, which also needs no GPU queue.

**Still waiting on you:**
1. **COLMAP:** should I submit the job on all 1,500 frames?
2. **Commit and push:** should I commit this branch and push it and `main`? Your teammates still don't have the rules or these scripts.

"""Estimate cameras and sparse points from ordered video frames with COLMAP.

    python scripts/reconstruct_colmap.py FRAMES_DIR OUT_DIR --vocab-tree VOCAB.bin

Uses sequential matching with loop detection. Keeps the largest model in OUT_DIR/sparse
and writes summary.json.
"""

import argparse
import json
import os
import time
from pathlib import Path

import pycolmap


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("frames_dir", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("out_dir", type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("--vocab-tree", type=Path, required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--overlap", type=int, default=20)
    parser.add_argument("--limit", type=int, help="use only the first N frames, for smoke tests")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    args.out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    names = sorted(path.name for path in args.frames_dir.glob("*.jpg"))[: args.limit]
    threads = len(os.sched_getaffinity(0))
    database = args.out_dir / "database.db"
    timings = {}

    start = time.perf_counter()
    reader = pycolmap.ImageReaderOptions()
    reader.camera_model = "OPENCV"
    extraction = pycolmap.FeatureExtractionOptions()
    extraction.num_threads = threads
    extraction.use_gpu = False
    pycolmap.extract_features(
        database,
        args.frames_dir,
        image_names=names,
        camera_mode=pycolmap.CameraMode.SINGLE,
        reader_options=reader,
        extraction_options=extraction,
    )
    timings["extract_seconds"] = round(time.perf_counter() - start)
    print(f"Extracted features: {timings['extract_seconds']} s", flush=True)

    start = time.perf_counter()
    matching = pycolmap.FeatureMatchingOptions()
    matching.num_threads = threads
    matching.use_gpu = False
    pairing = pycolmap.SequentialPairingOptions()
    pairing.overlap = args.overlap
    pairing.loop_detection = True
    pairing.vocab_tree_path = str(args.vocab_tree)
    pycolmap.match_sequential(database, matching_options=matching, pairing_options=pairing)
    timings["match_seconds"] = round(time.perf_counter() - start)
    print(f"Matched features: {timings['match_seconds']} s", flush=True)

    start = time.perf_counter()
    mapping = pycolmap.IncrementalPipelineOptions()
    mapping.num_threads = threads
    models = pycolmap.incremental_mapping(
        database, args.frames_dir, args.out_dir / "models", options=mapping
    )
    timings["map_seconds"] = round(time.perf_counter() - start)

    sizes = sorted((model.num_reg_images() for model in models.values()), reverse=True)
    summary = {"frames": len(names), "threads": threads, "model_sizes": sizes, **timings}
    if models:
        best = max(models.values(), key=lambda model: model.num_reg_images())
        sparse = args.out_dir / "sparse"
        sparse.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        best.write(sparse)
        best.export_PLY(args.out_dir / "points.ply")
        summary |= {
            "registered": best.num_reg_images(),
            "points3d": best.num_points3D(),
            "mean_reprojection_error_px": round(best.compute_mean_reprojection_error(), 3),
        }
    (args.out_dir / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))
    print(json.dumps(summary, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Agent guidelines

Since AI Hackathon 2026, 5-person team. Several people and agents work here at once.
This file is loaded with every prompt, so keep it short.

## Project status
- Main challenge: Valmet's Industrial Metaverse, semantic 3D scene understanding and a field-service
  copilot. Requirements and data problems: `docs/CHALLENGE.md`. Read it before pipeline work.
- Scene input is Valmet's `Industrial Boiler Room.ply`. Don't replace it with our own reconstruction
  unless Valmet has confirmed that's allowed. Keep it out of git.
- Scoring: asset extraction 30%, navigation 25%, AI diagnostics 20%, backend 15%, demo 10%. Put
  backend and spatial work first, keep the UI lightweight, and build no mobile app.
- Never invent asset identity. Store how each asset was mapped and with what confidence.
- Sponsor challenges are optional extras. Don't add a sponsor integration unless asked.

## Team areas
Stay in your person's area. Ask before making large changes in someone else's.

| Person | Area |
|---|---|
| TBD | TBD |

## Saving tokens
- Search first (`rg`, `git grep`), then read only the lines you need. Don't scan the whole repo.
- Don't read `uv.lock`, `data/`, `runs/`, or logs unless the task requires it. Use `tail` on logs.
- Don't re-read files you just edited, and don't repeat tool output back in replies.
- Keep replies short: what changed, what was verified, what's next.
- Use subagents only when a task truly needs them.
- Start a new session for each new task, and resume from the handoff instead of old chat.
- Use the cheapest model that can do the job.

## Git
- Never commit directly to `main`. It must always run, because it's what we demo.
- Before editing anything, check the current branch. If it's `main`, run `git pull`, then create a
  `name/feature` branch. Ask the user for their name if you can't tell it from `git config user.name`.
- Keep branches small and merge within a couple of hours.
- Rebase on `main` before opening a PR, and PR only when `make check` passes.
- Change `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` in their own small PR. Add packages with `uv add`.
- If running agents in parallel, give each its own git worktree.
- Never commit secrets (use `.env`, and list new names in `.env.example`), datasets, or checkpoints.
- Never force-push `main` or rewrite someone else's branch.

## Before finishing a prompt
1. If code changed, run `make check` and fix failures. Report failures you can't fix.
2. If files changed, update your handoff (below). Commit it together with your work.

## Handoff
Your file is `handoffs/<name>.md`, where `<name>` is `git config user.name`, lowercased, with
spaces replaced by hyphens. Overwrite it each time and keep it under 15 lines:

```markdown
# <name>: <branch>
**Goal:** what this work is for
**Done:** what changed, with key files
**Verified:** what was run, and the result
**Next:** the next concrete step
**Blockers:** anything stuck, or "none"
```

At the start of a session, read your own handoff. Read a teammate's only if your task touches
their area.

## Commands
| Command | Use |
|---|---|
| `make check` | Lint and test: run before finishing |
| `make lint` | Format check and ruff only (no torch needed) |
| `make test` | pytest |
| `make fmt` | Auto-fix style |
| `make train` | Train a model |

- Python 3.12, managed by uv. Use `uv run` and `uv add`, not `pip`.
- Put tests in `tests/`. Use `pytest.importorskip("torch")` for tests needing torch or other heavy
  dependencies, because CI runs without them.

## Compute
| Machine | Use for |
|---|---|
| ThinkPads | Coding and small CPU runs |
| RTX 5090 | Quick GPU training and experiments (shared, so check `nvidia-smi` first) |
| LUMI | Large jobs. AMD GPUs and no Docker: follow `lumi/README.md` |
| Roihu | Project `project_2020113`, work in `/scratch/project_2020113/sinceai`. x86 L40 GPUs via `vizinteractive` (12 h limit). GH200 nodes are ARM with a long queue |

## Hackathon rules
- Keep the README's "Pre-existing work" section accurate.
- A working demo beats clean abstractions. Avoid building for needs we don't have yet.

# Agent guidelines

Since AI Hackathon 2026, 5-person team. Several people and agents work here at once.
This file is loaded with every prompt, so keep it short.

## Project status
- Main challenge: Valmet's Industrial Metaverse, semantic 3D scene understanding and a field-service
  copilot. Requirements and data problems: `docs/CHALLENGE.md`. Read it before pipeline work.
- Scene input is Valmet's `Industrial Boiler Room.ply`. Don't replace it with our own reconstruction
  unless Valmet has confirmed that's allowed. Keep it out of git.
- Scoring: asset extraction 30%, navigation 25%, AI diagnostics 20%, backend 15%, demo 10%. Put
  backend and spatial work first, keep the UI lightweight, and build no mobile app.
- Never invent asset identity. Store how each asset was mapped and with what confidence.
- Sponsor challenges are optional extras. Don't add a sponsor integration unless asked.

## Team areas
Stay in your person's area. Ask before making large changes in someone else's.

| Person | Area |
|---|---|
| TBD | TBD |

## Saving tokens
- Search first (`rg`, `git grep`), then read only the lines you need. Don't scan the whole repo.
- Don't read `uv.lock`, `data/`, `runs/`, or logs unless the task requires it. Use `tail` on logs.
- Don't re-read files you just edited, and don't repeat tool output back in replies.
- Keep replies short: what changed, what was verified, what's next.
- Use subagents only when a task truly needs them.
- Start a new session for each new task, and resume from the handoff instead of old chat.
- Use the cheapest model that can do the job.

## Git
- Never commit directly to `main`. It must always run, because it's what we demo.
- Before editing anything, check the current branch. If it's `main`, run `git pull`, then create a
  `name/feature` branch. Ask the user for their name if you can't tell it from `git config user.name`.
- Keep branches small and merge within a couple of hours.
- Rebase on `main` before opening a PR, and PR only when `make check` passes.
- Change `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` in their own small PR. Add packages with `uv add`.
- If running agents in parallel, give each its own git worktree.
- Never commit secrets (use `.env`, and list new names in `.env.example`), datasets, or checkpoints.
- Never force-push `main` or rewrite someone else's branch.

## Before finishing a prompt
1. If code changed, run `make check` and fix failures. Report failures you can't fix.
2. If files changed, update your handoff (below). Commit it together with your work.

## Handoff
Your file is `handoffs/<name>.md`, where `<name>` is `git config user.name`, lowercased, with
spaces replaced by hyphens. Overwrite it each time and keep it under 15 lines:

```markdown
# <name>: <branch>
**Goal:** what this work is for
**Done:** what changed, with key files
**Verified:** what was run, and the result
**Next:** the next concrete step
**Blockers:** anything stuck, or "none"
```

At the start of a session, read your own handoff. Read a teammate's only if your task touches
their area.

## Commands
| Command | Use |
|---|---|
| `make check` | Lint and test: run before finishing |
| `make lint` | Format check and ruff only (no torch needed) |
| `make test` | pytest |
| `make fmt` | Auto-fix style |
| `make train` | Train a model |

- Python 3.12, managed by uv. Use `uv run` and `uv add`, not `pip`.
- Put tests in `tests/`. Use `pytest.importorskip("torch")` for tests needing torch or other heavy
  dependencies, because CI runs without them.

## Compute
| Machine | Use for |
|---|---|
| ThinkPads | Coding and small CPU runs |
| RTX 5090 | Quick GPU training and experiments (shared, so check `nvidia-smi` first) |
| LUMI | Large jobs. AMD GPUs and no Docker: follow `lumi/README.md` |
| Roihu | Project `project_2020113`, work in `/scratch/project_2020113/sinceai`. x86 L40 GPUs via `vizinteractive` (12 h limit). GH200 nodes are ARM with a long queue |

## Hackathon rules
- Keep the README's "Pre-existing work" section accurate.
- A working demo beats clean abstractions. Avoid building for needs we don't have yet.

# Challenge: Industrial Metaverse (Valmet)

Summary of the official brief, which is the docx in `Valmet_SinceAI2026 _1_/` (not in git).
Questions go to the Since AI Discord challenge channel.

## What to build
Focus on backend and spatial processing. No mobile app, and keep the UI lightweight.

1. **Extract assets:** detect and put 3D boxes around as many objects as possible in
   `Industrial Boiler Room.ply`.
2. **Map metadata:** link extracted assets to the Excel pack. Random or procedural mapping is
   allowed, with a pre-determined faulty target device.
3. **Navigate:** a worker or robot follows an automatic, collision-free route on the floor to the
   faulty device.
4. **Show nearby assets:** highlight 3D boxes and metadata for assets near the avatar as it moves.
5. **Diagnose:** on arrival, an AI assistant explains the fault and recommends next steps, grounded
   in the Excel pack.

## Scoring
| Weight | Criterion |
|---|---|
| 30% | Number and quality of extracted, 3D-framed assets mapped to metadata |
| 25% | Realistic obstacle-free navigation and proximity display |
| 20% | AI diagnostics, grounding and explainability |
| 15% | Backend architecture: structured, automated, modular |
| 10% | Demo clarity and innovation |

## Submission
- Working demo, runnable locally or clearly recorded
- Repo with a concise README and setup instructions
- 5-8 slides: extraction pipeline, pathfinding, metadata mapping, AI approach
- Demo video, 5 minutes maximum
- Brief technical note on models, libraries, and software

## Data
| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `Industrial Boiler Room (1).ply` | Gaussian splat, spherical harmonics degree 3 (45 `f_rest`) |
| `Industrial Boiler Room (1).mp4` | 1080p walkthrough, 3,352 frames, 112 s, no camera poses supplied |
| `semantic extraction demo 1/2` | Reference videos of the desired output (different sites) |
| `Valmet_..._Builder_Pack (1)...xlsx` | 30 assets, states, alarms, work orders, service cases, docs |

Asset classes: 12 control valves, 6 pumps, 6 motors, 3 pressure transmitters, 3 vibration sensors.
The pack is synthetic. Its `Scene_Anchors` coordinates are placeholders, not real scene positions.

AI answers must follow the pack's rules: `DOC-RAG-GUIDE` (name the asset, cite evidence IDs, give
confidence, separate observation from hypothesis), `DOC-FIELD-SAFETY` (recommend verification, not
autonomous action), and `DOC-3D-MAPPING` (never silently guess identity, so store how each asset
was mapped and with what confidence).

## Scene input rule
The brief requires a demonstrator "using" `Industrial Boiler Room.ply`, and the minimum demo must
"process" it. Its technical freedom covers languages and visualization tools, not the input scene.
Its starter package list doesn't mention `Industrial Boiler Room.mp4`, though the file was supplied.
Our own reconstruction from that video is not an approved replacement unless Valmet confirms it.

## Known data problems (as of 2026-11-06)
- **The PLY looks damaged.** Records 0-502,481 are valid (unit quaternions, plausible values). The
  other 1,003,654 records, 67% of the file, look like random bytes, including NaN and values near
  1e36. The file size matches its header. Cause unknown. SHA-256 starts `117195366421b07a`.
- **A non-corrupted PLY is on its way.** Validate it when it arrives, and re-check the extent below.
- **Until replaced, load only the first 502,482 records.** Of those, 35,635 have opacity above 0.5.
  Their extent is about 8.7 x 2.7 x 4.4 scene units, with y the thin axis (probably vertical), so
  this may be only part of the room.
- **Files the pack mentions are missing:** `telemetry_full_14d_30min.csv` (the workbook has a 3-day
  sample) and the 38 RAG markdown files (the workbook has 8 core docs).

# Agent guidelines

Since AI Hackathon 2026, 5-person team. Several people and agents work here at once.
This file is loaded with every prompt, so keep it short.

## Project status
- Main challenge: Valmet's Industrial Metaverse, semantic 3D scene understanding and a field-service
  copilot. Requirements and data problems: `docs/CHALLENGE.md`. Read it before pipeline work.
- Scene input is Valmet's restored `Equipment Room.ply`, not the damaged `Industrial Boiler Room`
  copy. Don't replace it with our own reconstruction unless Valmet confirms. Keep it out of git.
- Scoring: asset extraction 30%, navigation 25%, AI diagnostics 20%, backend 15%, demo 10%. Put
  backend and spatial work first, keep the UI lightweight, and build no mobile app.
- Never invent asset identity. Store how each asset was mapped and with what confidence.
- Sponsor challenges are optional extras. Don't add a sponsor integration unless asked.

## Team areas
Stay in your person's area. Ask before making large changes in someone else's.

| Person | Area |
|---|---|
| TBD | TBD |

## Saving tokens
- Search first (`rg`, `git grep`), then read only the lines you need. Don't scan the whole repo.
- Don't read `uv.lock`, `data/`, `runs/`, or logs unless the task requires it. Use `tail` on logs.
- Don't re-read files you just edited, and don't repeat tool output back in replies.
- Keep replies short: what changed, what was verified, what's next.
- Use subagents only when a task truly needs them.
- Start a new session for each new task, and resume from the handoff instead of old chat.
- Use the cheapest model that can do the job.

## Git
- Never commit directly to `main`. It must always run, because it's what we demo.
- Before editing anything, check the current branch. If it's `main`, run `git pull`, then create a
  `name/feature` branch. Ask the user for their name if you can't tell it from `git config user.name`.
- Keep branches small and merge within a couple of hours.
- Rebase on `main` before opening a PR, and PR only when `make check` passes.
- Change `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` in their own small PR. Add packages with `uv add`.
- If running agents in parallel, give each its own git worktree.
- Never commit secrets (use `.env`, and list new names in `.env.example`), datasets, or checkpoints.
- Never force-push `main` or rewrite someone else's branch.

## Before finishing a prompt
1. If code changed, run `make check` and fix failures. Report failures you can't fix.
2. If files changed, update your handoff (below). Commit it together with your work.

## Handoff
Your file is `handoffs/<name>.md`, where `<name>` is `git config user.name`, lowercased, with
spaces replaced by hyphens. Overwrite it each time and keep it under 15 lines:

```markdown
# <name>: <branch>
**Goal:** what this work is for
**Done:** what changed, with key files
**Verified:** what was run, and the result
**Next:** the next concrete step
**Blockers:** anything stuck, or "none"
```

At the start of a session, read your own handoff. Read a teammate's only if your task touches
their area.

## Commands
| Command | Use |
|---|---|
| `make check` | Lint and test: run before finishing |
| `make lint` | Format check and ruff only (no torch needed) |
| `make test` | pytest |
| `make fmt` | Auto-fix style |
| `make train` | Train a model |

- Python 3.12, managed by uv. Use `uv run` and `uv add`, not `pip`.
- Put tests in `tests/`. Use `pytest.importorskip("torch")` for tests needing torch or other heavy
  dependencies, because CI runs without them.

## Compute
| Machine | Use for |
|---|---|
| ThinkPads | Coding and small CPU runs |
| RTX 5090 | Quick GPU training and experiments (shared, so check `nvidia-smi` first) |
| LUMI | Large jobs. AMD GPUs and no Docker: follow `lumi/README.md` |
| Roihu | Project `project_2020113`, work in `/scratch/project_2020113/sinceai`. x86 L40 GPUs via `vizinteractive` (12 h limit). GH200 nodes are ARM with a long queue |

## Hackathon rules
- Keep the README's "Pre-existing work" section accurate.
- A working demo beats clean abstractions. Avoid building for needs we don't have yet.

# Challenge: Industrial Metaverse (Valmet)

Summary of the official brief, which is the docx in `Valmet_SinceAI2026 _1_/` (not in git).
Questions go to the Since AI Discord challenge channel.

## What to build
Focus on backend and spatial processing. No mobile app, and keep the UI lightweight.

1. **Extract assets:** detect and put 3D boxes around as many objects as possible in
   `Industrial Boiler Room.ply`.
2. **Map metadata:** link extracted assets to the Excel pack. Random or procedural mapping is
   allowed, with a pre-determined faulty target device.
3. **Navigate:** a worker or robot follows an automatic, collision-free route on the floor to the
   faulty device.
4. **Show nearby assets:** highlight 3D boxes and metadata for assets near the avatar as it moves.
5. **Diagnose:** on arrival, an AI assistant explains the fault and recommends next steps, grounded
   in the Excel pack.

## Scoring
| Weight | Criterion |
|---|---|
| 30% | Number and quality of extracted, 3D-framed assets mapped to metadata |
| 25% | Realistic obstacle-free navigation and proximity display |
| 20% | AI diagnostics, grounding and explainability |
| 15% | Backend architecture: structured, automated, modular |
| 10% | Demo clarity and innovation |

## Submission
- Working demo, runnable locally or clearly recorded
- Repo with a concise README and setup instructions
- 5-8 slides: extraction pipeline, pathfinding, metadata mapping, AI approach
- Demo video, 5 minutes maximum
- Brief technical note on models, libraries, and software

## Data
| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `Equipment Room.ply` | Restored Gaussian splat, spherical harmonics degree 3 (45 `f_rest`). Use this one |
| `Industrial Boiler Room (1).ply` | Damaged original. Don't use it |
| `Industrial Boiler Room (1).mp4` | 1080p walkthrough, 3,352 frames, 112 s, no camera poses supplied |
| `semantic extraction demo 1/2` | Reference videos of the desired output (different sites) |
| `Valmet_..._Builder_Pack (1)...xlsx` | 30 assets, states, alarms, work orders, service cases, docs |

Asset classes: 12 control valves, 6 pumps, 6 motors, 3 pressure transmitters, 3 vibration sensors.
The pack is synthetic. Its `Scene_Anchors` coordinates are placeholders, not real scene positions.

AI answers must follow the pack's rules: `DOC-RAG-GUIDE` (name the asset, cite evidence IDs, give
confidence, separate observation from hypothesis), `DOC-FIELD-SAFETY` (recommend verification, not
autonomous action), and `DOC-3D-MAPPING` (never silently guess identity, so store how each asset
was mapped and with what confidence).

## Scene input rule
The brief requires a demonstrator "using" `Industrial Boiler Room.ply`, and the minimum demo must
"process" it. Its technical freedom covers languages and visualization tools, not the input scene.

That's useful, as you can now pick whichever splat is better. `Equipment Room.ply` stays the default until yours beats it. So it hasn't formed one complete model so far, and that may or may not resolve by the end. I've restarted the watcher, so I'll report back when it finishes.

**How to choose the winner:** I'd run the same pipeline on both and compare the results, since looks alone won't tell you what scores:
| Check | What decides it |
|---|---|
| **Assets** | More distinct objects framed, and fewer junk boxes (30% of the score) |
| **Routing** | A connected floor and a route that doesn't clip through anything (25%) |
| **Coverage** | Fewer missing areas, especially around the pumps and tanks |
| **Visual quality** | Sharper views of the same spots, including pipes and labels |

Your own splat also has real advantages. You'd have exact camera poses for the real video frames, which should help SAM produce better masks. You could also train with more frames or iterations if the quality needs it.

**The plan:**
1. **Build on `Equipment Room.ply` now:** the loader, floor and extraction shouldn't wait for the reconstruction, and swapping scenes later only means re-running them.
2. **Train 3DGS if COLMAP gives a clean model:** it can run alongside that work. If COLMAP stays split, I'd try loading the largest model first, then Pi³X on about 150 frames as a fallback.
3. **Compare once extraction works:** that way you judge both on real asset counts.

**To keep this moving, I need your OK on two things:**
- **Commit and push:** can I do this now? Your teammates still don't have any of this.
- **Build the loader and cleaning step:** can I start that next?

content.text:
**Yes, it's essentially a navigable digital twin of the room, viewed in a tablet-friendly web app.** The twin part is real geometry from the splat plus synthetic device data, so it won't be live plant data unless you add that later.

## The tablet question
What the representative described and the written brief don't quite match:
- **The written brief:** it says not to spend time on a mobile or Android frontend, and its scoring favours backend and spatial work.
- **The representative:** they describe a person using it on a tablet. The Excel pack leans that way too, listing mobile/tablet use as a top-priority question.

**A web app that opens in a tablet's browser covers both.** You skip native Android, keep the UI light as the brief asks, and can still hand a judge a tablet. The heavy processing runs ahead of time, so the tablet mostly just displays the results.

## What the user sees
1. **Open the room:** the 3D scene appears with a frame around each detected object.
2. **Tap an object:** see its type, status and telemetry, plus recent alarms and documents. Objects with no matching Excel record simply show as detected objects.
3. **Tap "Navigate":** a collision-free route appears on the floor, and an avatar walks it.
4. **Pass things along the way:** nearby objects highlight and show their details.
5. **Arrive at the faulty device:** the AI explains the fault, cites its evidence, and suggests safe next checks.

Step 3 onward is the brief's required demo. Step 2, plus navigating to any object you choose, is what the representative added, and it needs very little extra work if the route planner accepts any target.

## How it's built
| Part | Job | When it runs |
|---|---|---|
| **Scene pipeline** | Load the splat, extract objects and boxes, build the floor map | Ahead of time, on Roihu or the 5090 |
| **Data mapping** | Link objects to Excel records, with a mapping confidence | Ahead of time |
| **Backend API** | Serve objects and details, plan routes, run the AI copilot | Live; the pack already suggests routes |
| **Web viewer** | Show the scene, boxes, route and details | Live, in the browser |

## Limits to be upfront about
- **No real-world positioning:** the app doesn't know where the person is standing, so navigation runs as a simulation from a chosen start point. Live tracking through QR codes or AR would be a stretch goal, as the pack's QR and NFC IDs are only synthetic.
- **Tablet performance is untested:** 1.7 million splats may be too heavy for a tablet. You'd probably need a reduced version of the scene, or a laptop as the fallback for the demo.
- **Viewer choice is still open:** I'd test Viser on a real tablet early. If its controls feel too limited, a small three.js page may be the better fit, though it's more work.

## One question for the representative
**Does the tablet experience count in judging, or is it just the long-term vision?** If it's the vision, a browser page that works on a tablet is enough. If it's judged, the viewer deserves more time, though I'd still put extraction and navigation first, since the written scoring gives them 55%.

The plan doesn't otherwise change: the loader and cleaning step still come first. Once you've got that answer, or if you want to start now, I can begin on the loader, and I still need your OK to commit and push.

# Plan

We're building a tablet-friendly web demo of a digital twin of the room. Each person can start now
against `fixtures/sample_assets.json`, then swap in real data as it's ready.

## The demo
1. Open the room: the 3D scene shows a frame around every detected object.
2. Tap an object: see its type, status, telemetry, alarms, and documents.
3. Tap "Navigate": a collision-free route appears and an avatar walks it.
4. Along the way, nearby objects highlight and show their details.
5. At the faulty device (`P-005`), the AI explains the fault, cites evidence, and suggests safe checks.

Requirements and scoring are in `docs/CHALLENGE.md`.

## Who does what
Swap freely if someone's skills fit another area better. Update this table and `AGENTS.md` if you do.

| Person | Area | Folder | Score |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Viktor** | Scene loading, cleaning, rendering, own splat | `app/scene/` | Enables all |
| **Sasha** | Asset extraction and 3D boxes | `app/extract/` | 30% |
| **Eduard** | Floor, routing, nearby search, backend API | `app/nav/`, `app/api/` | 25% + 15% |
| **Hannu** | Excel data, asset mapping, AI copilot | `app/copilot/` | 20% + part of 30% |
| **Benjamin** | Web viewer, tablet, demo video, slides | `web/`, `docs/` | 10% + 25% display |

## First tasks
**Viktor**
1. Write `app/scene/load.py`: read a splat PLY and filter it by opacity and size.
2. Render color and depth views with known cameras, for Sasha to use.
3. Check the COLMAP result, train 3DGS if it's clean, and compare it with `Equipment Room.ply`.

**Sasha**
1. Run SAM and CLIP on sample video frames to find which settings detect the most useful objects.
2. Project masks into 3D using Viktor's views, and merge them across views.
3. Write real `assets.json`, and count how many objects it finds.

**Eduard**
1. Build the API from the fixture, with the routes below, so Benjamin can connect straight away.
2. Write `app/nav/`: find the floor in `Equipment Room.ply` and build an occupancy grid.
3. Add A* routing with a body-width margin, then nearby search.

**Hannu**
1. Load the Excel workbook into a simple local store, and read its `DOC-RAG-GUIDE` rules.
2. Write `mapping.json`: match objects to records by class, with `P-005` as the faulty target.
3. Build the copilot: answers must cite event and document IDs, and give a confidence.

**Benjamin**
1. Test whether a real tablet can show the splat in Viser. Try a reduced scene if it struggles.
2. Choose Viser or a small three.js page, then show the fixture's boxes and details.
3. Add the route, walking avatar, and nearby highlights. Then own the video and 5-8 slides.

## Shared data
Generated files go in `data/scene/<scene_id>/`, which isn't in git. All coordinates use the original
scene's axes, so +y points down in `Equipment Room.ply`. Each file has one owner.

| File | Owner | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `assets.json` | Sasha | Objects with label, confidence, center, and box. See the fixture |
| `mapping.json` | Hannu | `object_id` to `asset_id`, `tag`, `method`, and `confidence` |
| `nav_grid.npz` | Eduard | Occupancy grid, origin, cell size, and floor height |

Objects with no Excel record keep `mapping: null` and show as detected objects. Never invent an ID.

## API
Eduard owns this, and it extends the Excel pack's `API_Contract` sheet. Agree changes with Benjamin.

| Route | Returns |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/assets` | All objects with boxes, mapping, and status |
| `GET /api/assets/{object_id}` | One object with telemetry, events, and documents |
| `GET /api/nearby?x=&y=&z=&radius=` | Objects near a point |
| `POST /api/route` with `start` and `object_id` | `path` (list of points) and `length` |
| `POST /api/copilot/query` with `object_id` and `question` | `answer`, `citations`, and `confidence` |

## Milestones
Check the submission deadline with the organizers, then adjust these.

| When | Goal |
|---|---|
| **Tonight** | Fixture works end to end: viewer, API, a fake route, and a stub copilot answer |
| **Saturday midday** | Real scene, real boxes, and a real route in the viewer |
| **Saturday evening** | Full demo on real data. Choose the scene. Stop adding features |
| **Sunday morning** | Fix bugs, record the video as a backup, finish slides and technical note |

## Getting started
- **Scene and data:** get `Equipment Room.ply` and the Valmet folder from Viktor, not from git.
- **Check your copy:** the SHA-256 of `Equipment Room.ply` starts `83d8c7d99316c08c`.
- **GPU:** the 5090 is shared. Roihu needs membership of `project_2020113`, so ask Viktor.
- **Merging:** merge small changes often, and tell the team when a shared file's format changes.
- **Tablet limit:** the app can't track a real person's position, so navigation is simulated.

# Agent guidelines

Since AI Hackathon 2026, 5-person team. Several people and agents work here at once.
This file is loaded with every prompt, so keep it short.

## Project status
- Main challenge: Valmet's Industrial Metaverse, semantic 3D scene understanding and a field-service
  copilot. Requirements and data problems: `docs/CHALLENGE.md`. Read it before pipeline work.
- Scene input is Valmet's restored `Equipment Room.ply`, not the damaged `Industrial Boiler Room`
  copy. Our own splat is allowed and replaces it only if it proves better. Keep scenes out of git.
- Keep pipeline code independent of which scene file it loads.
- Scoring: asset extraction 30%, navigation 25%, AI diagnostics 20%, backend 15%, demo 10%. Put
  backend and spatial work first, keep the UI lightweight, and build no mobile app.
- Never invent asset identity. Store how each asset was mapped and with what confidence.
- Sponsor challenges are optional extras. Don't add a sponsor integration unless asked.

## Team areas
Stay in your person's area. Ask before making large changes in someone else's.

| Person | Area |
|---|---|
| TBD | TBD |

## Saving tokens
- Search first (`rg`, `git grep`), then read only the lines you need. Don't scan the whole repo.
- Don't read `uv.lock`, `data/`, `runs/`, or logs unless the task requires it. Use `tail` on logs.
- Don't re-read files you just edited, and don't repeat tool output back in replies.
- Keep replies short: what changed, what was verified, what's next.
- Use subagents only when a task truly needs them.
- Start a new session for each new task, and resume from the handoff instead of old chat.
- Use the cheapest model that can do the job.

## Git
- Never commit directly to `main`. It must always run, because it's what we demo.
- Before editing anything, check the current branch. If it's `main`, run `git pull`, then create a
  `name/feature` branch. Ask the user for their name if you can't tell it from `git config user.name`.
- Keep branches small and merge within a couple of hours.
- Rebase on `main` before opening a PR, and PR only when `make check` passes.
- Change `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` in their own small PR. Add packages with `uv add`.
- If running agents in parallel, give each its own git worktree.
- Never commit secrets (use `.env`, and list new names in `.env.example`), datasets, or checkpoints.
- Never force-push `main` or rewrite someone else's branch.

## Before finishing a prompt
1. If code changed, run `make check` and fix failures. Report failures you can't fix.
2. If files changed, update your handoff (below). Commit it together with your work.

## Handoff
Your file is `handoffs/<name>.md`, where `<name>` is `git config user.name`, lowercased, with
spaces replaced by hyphens. Overwrite it each time and keep it under 15 lines:

```markdown
# <name>: <branch>
**Goal:** what this work is for
**Done:** what changed, with key files
**Verified:** what was run, and the result
**Next:** the next concrete step
**Blockers:** anything stuck, or "none"
```

At the start of a session, read your own handoff. Read a teammate's only if your task touches
their area.

## Commands
| Command | Use |
|---|---|
| `make check` | Lint and test: run before finishing |
| `make lint` | Format check and ruff only (no torch needed) |
| `make test` | pytest |
| `make fmt` | Auto-fix style |
| `make train` | Train a model |

- Python 3.12, managed by uv. Use `uv run` and `uv add`, not `pip`.
- Put tests in `tests/`. Use `pytest.importorskip("torch")` for tests needing torch or other heavy
  dependencies, because CI runs without them.

## Compute
| Machine | Use for |
|---|---|
| ThinkPads | Coding and small CPU runs |
| RTX 5090 | Quick GPU training and experiments (shared, so check `nvidia-smi` first) |
| LUMI | Large jobs. AMD GPUs and no Docker: follow `lumi/README.md` |
| Roihu | Project `project_2020113`, work in `/scratch/project_2020113/sinceai`. x86 L40 GPUs via `vizinteractive` (12 h limit). GH200 nodes are ARM with a long queue |

## Hackathon rules
- Keep the README's "Pre-existing work" section accurate.
- A working demo beats clean abstractions. Avoid building for needs we don't have yet.

# Plan

We're building a tablet-friendly web demo of a digital twin of the room. Each person can start now
against `fixtures/sample_assets.json`, then swap in real data as it's ready.

## The demo
1. Open the room: the 3D scene shows a frame around every detected object.
2. Tap an object: see its type, status, telemetry, alarms, and documents.
3. Tap "Navigate": a collision-free route appears and an avatar walks it.
4. Along the way, nearby objects highlight and show their details.
5. At the faulty device (`P-005`), the AI explains the fault, cites evidence, and suggests safe checks.

Requirements and scoring are in `docs/CHALLENGE.md`.

## Who does what
Swap freely if someone's skills fit another area better. Update this table and `AGENTS.md` if you do.

| Person | Area | Folder | Score |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Viktor** | Scene loading, cleaning, rendering, own splat | `app/scene/` | Enables all |
| **Sasha** | Asset extraction and 3D boxes | `app/extract/` | 30% |
| **Eduard** | Floor, routing, nearby search, backend API | `app/nav/`, `app/api/` | 25% + 15% |
| **Hannu** | Excel data, asset mapping, AI copilot | `app/copilot/` | 20% + part of 30% |
| **Benjamin** | Web viewer, tablet, demo video, slides | `web/`, `docs/` | 10% + 25% display |

## First tasks
**Viktor**
1. Write `app/scene/load.py`: read a splat PLY and filter it by opacity and size.
2. Render color and depth views with known cameras, for Sasha to use.
3. Check the COLMAP result, train 3DGS if it's clean, and compare it with `Equipment Room.ply`.

**Sasha**
1. Run SAM and CLIP on sample video frames to find which settings detect the most useful objects.
2. Project masks into 3D using Viktor's views, and merge them across views.
3. Write real `assets.json`, and count how many objects it finds.

**Eduard**
1. Build the API from the fixture, with the routes below, so Benjamin can connect straight away.
2. Write `app/nav/`: find the floor in `Equipment Room.ply` and build an occupancy grid.
3. Add A* routing with a body-width margin, then nearby search.

**Hannu**
1. Load the Excel workbook into a simple local store, and read its `DOC-RAG-GUIDE` rules.
2. Write `mapping.json`: match objects to records by class, with `P-005` as the faulty target.
3. Build the copilot: answers must cite event and document IDs, and give a confidence.

**Benjamin**
1. Test whether a real tablet can show the splat in Viser. Try a reduced scene if it struggles.
2. Choose Viser or a small three.js page, then show the fixture's boxes and details.
3. Add the route, walking avatar, and nearby highlights. Then own the video and 5-8 slides.

## Shared data
Generated files go in `data/scene/<scene_id>/`, which isn't in git. All coordinates use the original
scene's axes, so +y points down in `Equipment Room.ply`. Each file has one owner.

Objects with no Excel record keep `mapping: null` and show as detected objects. Never invent an ID.

## API
Eduard owns this, and it extends the Excel pack's `API_Contract` sheet. Agree changes with Benjamin.

| Route | Returns |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/assets` | All objects with boxes, mapping, and status |
| `GET /api/assets/{object_id}` | One object with telemetry, events, and documents |
| `GET /api/nearby?x=&y=&z=&radius=` | Objects near a point |
| `POST /api/route` with `start` and `object_id` | `path` (list of points) and `length` |
| `POST /api/copilot/query` with `object_id` and `question` | `answer`, `citations`, and `confidence` |

Check the submission deadline with the organizers, then adjust these.

| When | Goal |
|---|---|
| **Tonight** | Fixture works end to end: viewer, API, a fake route, and a stub copilot answer |
| **Saturday midday** | Real scene, real boxes, and a real route in the viewer |
| **Saturday evening** | Full demo on real data. Choose the scene. Stop adding features |
| **Sunday morning** | Fix bugs, record the video as a backup, finish slides and technical note |

content.text:
The pipeline has two halves. An **offline** half runs once ahead of time to turn the raw scene into data files, and a **live** half uses those files while someone taps around the app.

```text
OFFLINE (Roihu or 5090)
Splat (.ply) → clean → render views → SAM + CLIP → 3D boxes  → assets.json
                  │                                               │
                  │                                Excel pack → mapping.json
                  └─ floor + obstacles → occupancy grid → nav_grid.npz

LIVE (backend + browser)
Tablet viewer ⇄ Backend API ⇄ route planner, device data, AI copilot
```

## Offline: from raw scene to data files
1. **Load and clean (Viktor):** read `Equipment Room.ply` or your own splat, then remove nearly transparent or oversized splats that would act as false obstacles. The original coordinates stay as they are, so everything lines up in the viewer.
2. **Render views (Viktor):** place virtual cameras through the room and render colour and depth images. Because you choose the cameras, you know exactly where each pixel sits in 3D.
3. **Find objects (Sasha):**
    - SAM outlines every object it can find in each view.
    - CLIP names each outline, like "pump" or "ladder".
    - Each outline is projected into 3D using its depth.
    - Detections of the same object from different views are merged, and a box is fitted around each one.
    - The result is `assets.json`.
4. **Map device data (Hannu):** match objects to the 30 Excel records by class, so a detected pump gets a pump record. The brief allows this mapping to be procedural, so it's stored with its method and a low confidence. One pump becomes the faulty `P-005`, and objects with no match stay as plain detected objects. The result is `mapping.json`.
5. **Build the floor map (Eduard):**
    - Fit the floor plane.
    - Mark any cell with points at body height as blocked.
    - Widen obstacles by a body-width margin.
    - Keep only the floor area connected to the start point.
    - The result is `nav_grid.npz`.

## Live: what happens when someone uses it
1. **Open the room:** the viewer loads the splat (possibly a reduced version on a tablet), and `GET /api/assets` supplies the boxes, labels and statuses.
2. **Tap an object:** the API joins that object's mapping with its Excel telemetry, alarms and documents.
3. **Tap "Navigate":** `POST /api/route` runs A* on the grid from the start point to free floor beside the object, and returns a path of points. A machine's own cell is blocked, so the route stops next to it.
4. **Walk the route:** the avatar follows the path. As it moves, `GET /api/nearby` (or the same check in the browser) highlights nearby objects and shows their details.
5. **Arrive at the fault:** `POST /api/copilot/query` retrieves `P-005`'s telemetry, alarms, past service cases and documents, and passes them to the LLM. The answer names the asset, cites evidence IDs, gives a confidence, separates what's observed from what's suspected, and suggests a safe next check.

## Where your own splat fits
It's only an alternative input to step 1:

**Video → 1,500 frames → COLMAP cameras → 3DGS → your own `.ply`**

Then everything runs again on it, and you keep whichever scene gives better boxes and routes. That's why the pipeline code mustn't depend on one specific file.

## Where it's most likely to break
| Risk | Why | Backup |
|---|---|---|
| **Rendered views are blurry** | SAM and CLIP may do worse on splat renders than on real photos | Use real video frames with COLMAP cameras, if that run succeeds |
| **Object labels are wrong** | CLIP may struggle on industrial equipment | Show low confidence honestly, and hand-check the objects along the demo route |
| **Floor has gaps or clutter** | Routes may break or look wrong | Fill small gaps, and tune the height band and margin |
| **Splat too heavy on tablet** | Rendering may stutter | Use a reduced scene, or run the demo on a laptop |

Rendering and label quality are unproven until Sasha and I try them, so test them early. The route and copilot steps use well-known methods, so they should be less risky, though neither has been tested on this scene yet.

# Agent guidelines

Since AI Hackathon 2026, 5-person team. Several people and agents work here at once.
This file is loaded with every prompt, so keep it short.

## Project status
- Main challenge: Valmet's Industrial Metaverse, semantic 3D scene understanding and a field-service
  copilot. Requirements and data problems: `docs/CHALLENGE.md`. Read it before pipeline work.
- Scene input is Valmet's restored `Equipment Room.ply`, not the damaged `Industrial Boiler Room`
  copy. Our own splat is allowed and replaces it only if it proves better. Keep scenes out of git.
- Keep pipeline code independent of which scene file it loads.
- Scoring: asset extraction 30%, navigation 25%, AI diagnostics 20%, backend 15%, demo 10%. Put
  backend and spatial work first, keep the UI lightweight, and build no mobile app.
- Never invent asset identity. Store how each asset was mapped and with what confidence.
- Sponsor challenges are optional extras. Don't add a sponsor integration unless asked.

## Team areas
Stay in your person's area. Ask before making large changes in someone else's.

| Person | Area |
|---|---|
| Viktor | Scene loading, cleaning, rendering, own splat (`app/scene/`) |
| Sasha | Asset extraction and 3D boxes (`app/extract/`) |
| Eduard | Floor, routing, nearby search, backend API (`app/nav/`, `app/api/`) |
| Hannu | Excel data, asset mapping, AI copilot (`app/copilot/`) |
| Benjamin | Web viewer, tablet, demo video, slides (`web/`, `docs/`) |

Tasks, shared data formats, and API: `docs/PLAN.md`. Build against `fixtures/sample_assets.json`.

## Saving tokens
- Search first (`rg`, `git grep`), then read only the lines you need. Don't scan the whole repo.
- Don't read `uv.lock`, `data/`, `runs/`, or logs unless the task requires it. Use `tail` on logs.
- Don't re-read files you just edited, and don't repeat tool output back in replies.
- Keep replies short: what changed, what was verified, what's next.
- Use subagents only when a task truly needs them.
- Start a new session for each new task, and resume from the handoff instead of old chat.
- Use the cheapest model that can do the job.

## Git
- Never commit directly to `main`. It must always run, because it's what we demo.
- Before editing anything, check the current branch. If it's `main`, run `git pull`, then create a
  `name/feature` branch. Ask the user for their name if you can't tell it from `git config user.name`.
- Keep branches small and merge within a couple of hours.
- Rebase on `main` before opening a PR, and PR only when `make check` passes.
- Change `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` in their own small PR. Add packages with `uv add`.
- If running agents in parallel, give each its own git worktree.
- Never commit secrets (use `.env`, and list new names in `.env.example`), datasets, or checkpoints.
- Never force-push `main` or rewrite someone else's branch.

## Before finishing a prompt
1. If code changed, run `make check` and fix failures. Report failures you can't fix.
2. If files changed, update your handoff (below). Commit it together with your work.

## Handoff
Your file is `handoffs/<name>.md`, where `<name>` is `git config user.name`, lowercased, with
spaces replaced by hyphens. Overwrite it each time and keep it under 15 lines:

```markdown
# <name>: <branch>
**Goal:** what this work is for
**Done:** what changed, with key files
**Verified:** what was run, and the result
**Next:** the next concrete step
**Blockers:** anything stuck, or "none"
```

At the start of a session, read your own handoff. Read a teammate's only if your task touches
their area.

## Commands
| Command | Use |
|---|---|
| `make check` | Lint and test: run before finishing |
| `make lint` | Format check and ruff only (no torch needed) |
| `make test` | pytest |
| `make fmt` | Auto-fix style |
| `make train` | Train a model |

- Python 3.12, managed by uv. Use `uv run` and `uv add`, not `pip`.
- Put tests in `tests/`. Use `pytest.importorskip("torch")` for tests needing torch or other heavy
  dependencies, because CI runs without them.

## Compute
| Machine | Use for |
|---|---|
| ThinkPads | Coding and small CPU runs |
| RTX 5090 | Quick GPU training and experiments (shared, so check `nvidia-smi` first) |
| LUMI | Large jobs. AMD GPUs and no Docker: follow `lumi/README.md` |
| Roihu | Project `project_2020113`, work in `/scratch/project_2020113/sinceai`. x86 L40 GPUs via `vizinteractive` (12 h limit). GH200 nodes are ARM with a long queue |

## Hackathon rules
- Keep the README's "Pre-existing work" section accurate.
- A working demo beats clean abstractions. Avoid building for needs we don't have yet.

# Plan

We're building a tablet-friendly web demo of a digital twin of the room. Each person can start now
against `fixtures/sample_assets.json`, then swap in real data as it's ready.

## The demo
1. Open the room: the 3D scene shows a frame around every detected object.
2. Tap an object: see its type, status, telemetry, alarms, and documents.
3. Tap "Navigate": a collision-free route appears and an avatar walks it.
4. Along the way, nearby objects highlight and show their details.
5. At the faulty device (`P-005`), the AI explains the fault, cites evidence, and suggests safe checks.

Requirements and scoring are in `docs/CHALLENGE.md`.

## Who does what
Swap freely if someone's skills fit another area better. Update this table and `AGENTS.md` if you do.

| Person | Area | Folder | Score |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Viktor** | Scene loading, cleaning, rendering, own splat | `app/scene/` | Enables all |
| **Sasha** | Asset extraction and 3D boxes | `app/extract/` | 30% |
| **Eduard** | Floor, routing, nearby search, backend API | `app/nav/`, `app/api/` | 25% + 15% |
| **Hannu** | Excel data, asset mapping, AI copilot | `app/copilot/` | 20% + part of 30% |
| **Benjamin** | Web viewer, tablet, demo video, slides | `web/`, `docs/` | 10% + 25% display |

## First tasks
**Viktor**
1. Write `app/scene/load.py`: read a splat PLY and filter it by opacity and size.
2. Render color and depth views with known cameras, for Sasha to use.
3. Check the COLMAP result, train 3DGS if it's clean, and compare it with `Equipment Room.ply`.

**Sasha**
1. Run SAM and CLIP on sample video frames to find which settings detect the most useful objects.
2. Project masks into 3D using Viktor's views, and merge them across views.
3. Write real `assets.json`, and count how many objects it finds.

**Eduard**
1. Build the API from the fixture, with the routes below, so Benjamin can connect straight away.
2. Write `app/nav/`: find the floor in `Equipment Room.ply` and build an occupancy grid.
3. Add A* routing with a body-width margin, then nearby search.

**Hannu**
1. Load the Excel workbook into a simple local store, and read its `DOC-RAG-GUIDE` rules.
2. Write `mapping.json`: match objects to records by class, with `P-005` as the faulty target.
3. Build the copilot: answers must cite event and document IDs, and give a confidence.

**Benjamin**
1. Test whether a real tablet can show the splat in Viser. Try a reduced scene if it struggles.
2. Choose Viser or a small three.js page, then show the fixture's boxes and details.
3. Add the route, walking avatar, and nearby highlights. Then own the video and 5-8 slides.

## Shared data
Generated files go in `data/scene/<scene_id>/`, which isn't in git. All coordinates use the original
scene's axes, so +y points down in `Equipment Room.ply`. Each file has one owner.

| File | Owner | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `assets.json` | Sasha | Objects with label, confidence, center, and box. See the fixture |
| `mapping.json` | Hannu | `object_id` to `asset_id`, `tag`, `method`, and `confidence` |
| `nav_grid.npz` | Eduard | Occupancy grid, origin, cell size, and floor height |

Objects with no Excel record keep `mapping: null` and show as detected objects. Never invent an ID.

## API
Eduard owns this, and it extends the Excel pack's `API_Contract` sheet. Agree changes with Benjamin.

| Route | Returns |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/assets` | All objects with boxes, mapping, and status |
| `GET /api/assets/{object_id}` | One object with telemetry, events, and documents |
| `GET /api/nearby?x=&y=&z=&radius=` | Objects near a point |
| `POST /api/route` with `start` and `object_id` | `path` (list of points) and `length` |
| `POST /api/copilot/query` with `object_id` and `question` | `answer`, `citations`, and `confidence` |

## Milestones
Check the submission deadline with the organizers, then adjust these.

| When | Goal |
|---|---|
| **Tonight** | Fixture works end to end: viewer, API, a fake route, and a stub copilot answer |
| **Saturday midday** | Real scene, real boxes, and a real route in the viewer |
| **Saturday evening** | Full demo on real data. Choose the scene. Stop adding features |
| **Sunday morning** | Fix bugs, record the video as a backup, finish slides and technical note |

## Getting started
- **Scene and data:** get `Equipment Room.ply` and the Valmet folder from Viktor, not from git.
- **Check your copy:** the SHA-256 of `Equipment Room.ply` starts `83d8c7d99316c08c`.
- **GPU:** the 5090 is shared. Roihu needs membership of `project_2020113`, so ask Viktor.
- **Merging:** merge small changes often, and tell the team when a shared file's format changes.
- **Tablet limit:** the app can't track a real person's position, so navigation is simulated.

# Plan

against `fixtures/sample_assets.json`, then swap in real data as it's ready.

## The demo
1. Open the room: the 3D scene shows a frame around every detected object.
2. Tap an object: see its type, status, telemetry, alarms, and documents.
3. Tap "Navigate": a collision-free route appears and an avatar walks it.
4. Along the way, nearby objects highlight and show their details.
5. At the faulty device (`P-005`), the AI explains the fault, cites evidence, and suggests safe checks.

Requirements and scoring are in `docs/CHALLENGE.md`.

## Runs entirely on site
Plant data never leaves the site, which is a key selling point. One RTX 5090 server does the offline
processing and serves the app, and the tablet connects to it over the local network.

- **Copilot:** use a local LLM and local embeddings, sharing the 5090's memory with everything else.

content.text:
I'd build it this way: everything runs on a 5090 on site, and the tablet connects to it over the local network. **Just don't expect formal bonus points**, because the brief's scoring has no privacy criterion. It would mainly help under "demo clarity & innovation" (10%) and as a strong pitch for plants that can't send data off site. It's also an easy thing to prove live: unplug the internet and run the demo.

I've added this as a rule in [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) and [docs/PLAN.md](docs/PLAN.md), still uncommitted.

## What changes
| Area | Change |
|---|---|
| **Copilot (Hannu)** | A local LLM and local embeddings replace any cloud API. This is the biggest change |
| **Viewer (Benjamin)** | Libraries and fonts are served from the 5090, with no CDN links |
| **Offline pipeline (Viktor, Sasha)** | Must also run on the 5090, with models downloaded ahead of time |
| **Sponsor prizes** | Gemini and ElevenLabs's hosted APIs would break the rule, so skip them in the demo |
| **Roihu** | Fine for experiments, but say "the final pipeline runs on the 5090" only once it has actually run there |

## What it could improve
- **Tablet performance:** the 5090 could render the scene and stream video to the tablet, so the tablet doesn't have to handle 1.7 million splats. It's more work, so I'd only try it if Benjamin's reduced scene struggles.
- **Copilot reliability:** there's no dependency on event Wi-Fi or API limits during judging.

## Risks
- **GPU memory:** the 5090's memory has to hold the LLM and any live rendering. Heavy offline jobs like SAM and 3DGS should run before the demo, not during it.
- **Answer quality:** a local model will probably be weaker than the best cloud models. Tight retrieval and the required citations should help a lot, because the answers come from a small set of Excel data. Hannu should test this early, with the model size chosen to leave room for everything else.
- **Tablet connection:** it needs a reliable local link, so bring your own router and don't count on venue Wi-Fi.
- **Hidden internet use:** libraries can quietly download models or scripts at runtime. An offline rehearsal will catch that, and Eduard owns that check in the plan.

**The 5090 will be busy:** the team is sharing it for development, and it's now the demo machine too. Agree on a time to stop running experiments on it before the final rehearsal.

Everything is still waiting on your OK: **should I commit this, merge it into `main` and push it?** Your teammates can't start until then.

content.text:
**Yes, both could help, mostly with labelling objects.** Qwen also suits the on-site rule, as many of its models can run locally. Its vision models (Qwen-VL) handle images and text, so one model might cover both labelling and the copilot. Check the newest versions and their licences before choosing, as I haven't tested any on this data.

I told you earlier to drop OCR, but that was only about linking objects to Excel IDs. Since mapping can be random, OCR can't help there, but it's still useful for describing what each object actually is.

## Where each one helps
| Use | How | Benefit |
|---|---|---|
| **Better labels (VLM)** | Show it a crop from SAM and ask for the object type, chosen from a set list | Likely more accurate than CLIP on industrial equipment, which helps the 30% score |
| **Richer details (VLM)** | Ask for a short description and visible features | Objects with no Excel record still get useful info on tap |
| **Reading real text (OCR or VLM)** | Read text in the room, like "Grundfos" or "reflex" | Real evidence that makes the twin feel specific to this room |
| **Better mapping** | Match Excel records using the improved labels | A pump record lands on something that looks like a pump, and it supports the pack's "upgrade mapping with CV/VLM" question |
| **Copilot context (stretch)** | Give the copilot the object's description and a crop | It can say what's visible at the device, marked as an observation |

## Where it fits in the pipeline
This would be an extra offline step after SAM:

**SAM mask → best views of each object → VLM → type, confidence, visible text → `assets.json`**

- **Keep CLIP as the first pass:** it's fast, so use it across all masks. Send only the kept, merged objects to the VLM, so it doesn't spend time on every mask.
- **Run it ahead of time:** the results are saved, so the demo doesn't need to keep this model loaded unless the copilot uses it. That also frees up GPU memory.
- **Start with VLM only:** add a dedicated local OCR tool like PaddleOCR only if the VLM misreads text.

## Things to watch
- **Made-up answers:** a VLM can confidently invent labels or text. Limit it to a set list plus "unknown", ask for text exactly as written, and keep a confidence. Don't treat a brand it reads as proof of an Excel identity.
- **Image quality:** text needs sharp images, so use real video frames, which also needs COLMAP cameras if you want them tied to 3D positions. Splat renders will probably blur small text, and 1080p with motion blur will limit it too.
- **Measure before adopting:** hand-label about 20–30 objects, then compare CLIP and the VLM. Only keep the VLM if it's clearly better, and those same numbers can go in your slides.

## Who does it
- **Sasha:** VLM labelling and text reading, after SAM boxes work. Boxes come first, because a better label is no use until the object has been found.
- **Hannu:** chooses the copilot model, and tests whether a Qwen-VL model is good enough to serve both jobs.

Want me to add this to [docs/PLAN.md](docs/PLAN.md)? And I still need your OK to commit, merge and push, as your teammates can't start until then.
